rv.q: Jennings and Duncan are well matched and the dialogue — that Lady Tebbit remark and some forced references to Carol Thatcher aside — displays some wit.
I can't help feeling that – presented this year, this autumn, this week, when all eyes are on Westminster – the piece fails to answer the serendipitous tantalisation of its title.
Thanks to a strong finish and a world-class cast and creative team, 'Hansard' is solid enough.
It's a rabbit-out-of-the-hat moment that only partly redeems what's gone before.
So although there is much to enjoy in Simon Godwin's production, the play's ending feels oddly incomplete.
Well-crafted and well-acted as the play is, it's hard to warm to it.
With such a pair of consummate, on-stage professionals to deliver a script which has been fine-tuned like a Bentley, director Simon Godwin must have felt charmed landing the gig.
There's some excellent acting in this intriguing and combative production.
I wasn't convinced that the final scenes were psychologically consistent with the prickly wordplay of the earlier sections.

What it's all meant to add up to is anyone's guess, beyond the sneaking suspicion that Mr. Woods wanted to write a play about today's intensifying political divide from the safety of a period that may not be as vanished as you might think.
Hansard is an entertaining if cynical look at the personal lives of a politician's family, and the pressures that brings, but more so it's a profile of these two nasty people scarred by their pasts.
Hansard is a great political play, one that tells us everything about the society we have become and why the impasse of the last three years cannot be easily broken.

Unfortunately, the final revelations in this 90-minute play come about 20 minutes too late, and Woods's inexperience shows: he has simply not given himself enough time to fully excavate the psychological conflicts that he has so neatly introduced.
In general, for me this play just doesn't hit its mark. It feels somewhat aimless and undercooked, without much of a foundation to build itself on.

cn.t: A polished two-hander elevated by stellar performances from Duncan and Jennings, though critics find Woods' debut play derivative and overfamiliar, with most praising the acting over the Albee-esque writing.
